analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and puts the old health care rules back in place.
analysis.headline: The repeal bill never advanced past committee referral and died when the 111th Congress ended, leaving the Affordable Care Act in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the Affordable Care Act — the 2010 health care law that expanded insurance coverage, created marketplaces with subsidies, banned insurers from denying coverage for pre-existing conditions, and imposed taxes on high earners and health industries — effective as if it had never passed. It was introduced a few months after the law was enacted by a Democratic Congress and was referred to eight House committees. It never received a hearing or a vote and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers, drug and device makers, and higher-income households, all of whom faced new taxes, fees, or regulatory requirements under the ACA; repeal would have removed those costs. People who preferred the pre-2010 insurance market's lower-premium, skimpier plans would also have regained that option.

how_it_helps.text: It would have eliminated the ACA's taxes and mandates, which fell in part on higher-income households, drug and device makers, and health insurers.
It would have freed health insurers from the law's coverage requirements, minimum medical loss ratios, and other new regulations.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost: losing coverage expansions, subsidies, protections for pre-existing conditions, and the option to stay on a parent's plan, with millions more left uninsured.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients, especially the uninsured and sick

drawbacks.text: Repealing the law would have taken away coverage expansions and subsidies, restoring the pre-2010 system in which millions more Americans were uninsured and insurers could deny coverage for pre-existing conditions.
The bill offered no replacement; it simply restored the law as it stood before the ACA, leaving the gaps that led to the reform in place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had no practical benefit: with Democrats controlling the House, it never had a chance and did not advance beyond referral to subcommittees. Its costs, had it passed, would have been large — stripping coverage protections, subsidies, and regulations from millions of people — while its gains went mainly to the health insurance industry and high-income households.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to committees and then to subcommittees, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 13, 2010 and referred to eight House committees, then to two health-related subcommittees.
No further action was taken before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, so the bill never received a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Millions of people who had just gained coverage and protections under the new health law, since it stayed on the books. Health insurers also kept the new customers the law's rules and subsidies created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The newly insured; ACA stayed law

for.name: Rep. Parker Griffith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Affordable Care Act.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans; the Democratic House majority never acted on the bill.

industries.note: Repeal would have ended the law's coverage expansions, subsidies, and protections for people with pre-existing conditions, restoring the pre-2010 system where millions went without coverage. This is an interest, not an industry, but it is the largest loser.
Repeal would have freed insurers from new federal rules on coverage, enrollment, and medical spending, while leaving them the gatekeepers of coverage as before.
The ACA included a Medicare payroll surtax on high earners and an investment-income surtax; repeal as of enactment would have restored the pre-ACA tax code for them.
